maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING PROPRIETY OF CERTAIN QUESTIONS APPEARING ON THE ORDER PAPER

speechtext:
On the orders of the day.
Right hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):	Recently on a
matter of privilege I drew attention to the appearance on the order paper of certain questions which to my mind should not have been permitted to be placed on the records of the house. To-day one of these questions continues to appear on the order paper. It is under date May 15, and is question 23, asked by Mr. Lafleche. It is as follows:
1.	During the term of office of Hon. Rodolphe Lemieux, as Speaker of the House of Commons, were certain pieces of furniture, the property of the state, transported to his summer residence, at Point an Pic, Quebec?
2.	If so, what were said pieces of furniture?
3.	Has said furniture been returned?
4.	If so, at whose request?
5.	Who paid for the transportation of the said furniture?
To any one not familiar with the facts the question I have read would, I submit, leave the impression that certain furniture had been taken by the former Speaker from the House of Commons to his summer residence, had been brought back to the speaker's apartment in the city and that transportation had been paid by the state. To-day the Hon Senator Lemieux called upon me at my office and asked me to make the very positive statement that at no time was any furniture taken from the Speaker's apartment to his summer home during his term of office or at any other time, and of course that there was no transportation of furniture one way or the other at the expense of the state. If the question in the form it is put were not protected by the privileges of parliament it would constitute a libellous statement.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING PROPRIETY OF CERTAIN QUESTIONS APPEARING ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING PROPRIETY OF CERTAIN QUESTIONS APPEARING ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext: It is equivalent to such.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING PROPRIETY OF CERTAIN QUESTIONS APPEARING ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext: Oh, no.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING PROPRIETY OF CERTAIN QUESTIONS APPEARING ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Any person
reading the question would consider it a very serious reflection upon the character of the former Speaker of the House of Commons. I do not think it should be allowed to remain on the order paper, particularly in view of the statements I am now making to the house in the name of the former Speaker as to the true facts of the case.
In the same connection, to indicate the injustice of these questions, simply as questions, I would say that yesterday a question was answered relating amongst other matters to the automobile used by the former Speaker. One would have thought from the wording of the question that the automobile used by the former Speaker had been the property of the state, whereas, as a matter of fact, the answer to the question made clear the fact that the automobile was the personal property of the Speaker himself. It was

Privilege-Mr. Mackenzie King
purchased by the Speaker himself. Meanwhile owing to headlines in the press arising out of the question a different impression has gone abroad, one which the reply may never serve to overtake. Similarly there has been a question regarding the payment of servants of the former Speaker. The hon. Senator Lemieux advises me that before he assumed the office of Speaker he obtained from the Sergeant at Arms a memorandum with respect to the staff of His Honour the Speaker and the perquisites of the office generally and that during his term of office he acted entirely in accordance with the memorandum then given to him, a copy of which I have in my hand at the present time. As Your Honour knows in former years the residence of the Speaker was part of these houses of parliament. After the fire which destroyed the then House of Commons and incidentally the residence of the Speaker, His Honour the Speaker made use of a private residence as the residence of the Speaker, but was allowed some equivalent for service and the like. If a definite allowance were not given, certain perquisites were allowed with respect to servants and other incidentals in an attempt to equalize the position of the Speaker as it had existed formerly when the premises of the Speaker were connected immediately with the House of Commons. As regards servants employed, the then Speaker was but following the traditions of the house since we have had a parliament. It is a great shame that questions of the kind, which through what they carry in the way of innuendo reflect upon one who was three times elected speaker of this house, should be permitted to be circulated through the press, and I would ask that certainly as respects the one question which remains Your Honour give instructions that it be deleted from the records of the house.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. MACKENZIE KING PROPRIETY OF CERTAIN QUESTIONS APPEARING ON THE ORDER PAPER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that you or anyone else has the right to delete from the order paper of parliament any question that affects the expenditure of public moneys. One may doubt the propriety of putting the questions, but three of them touch the expenditure of public moneys. The Auditor General's report will indicate who got the moneys and what they were spent for, and the circumstances may be inquired into by the public accounts committee. It may not be desirable-and with respect to that I think perhaps there is a little difference of opinion between the right hon. gentleman (Mr. Mackenzie King) and myself-to make inquiries by way of questions as to these expenditures when the method for doing so

is provided through the public accounts committee, where it may be determined what moneys have been expended in connection with the maintenance of the Speaker's quarters and the circumstances under which they were so expended. I would certainly think that that was a matter which being in the Auditor General's report should be dealt with before the public accounts committee.
Question 23 has now been answered by the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). I do not think it is a proper question, for another reason altogether-that there is nobody I know of who would be in a position to answer it except the former Speaker himself, unless it be some official of the House of Commons.
In that regard it may be explained that there was some feeling in this country last year in connection with the attitude of the former Speaker of this chamber, who retained the exercise of his powers as Speaker even after he had become a senator and who participated in the campaign which culminated in the election of July 28. I can readily understand the curiosity of people, whether legitimate or not, to determine if the former Speaker, having been appointed to the upper house of this parliament, was continuing to exercise control over the expenditures of this house. That question has been seriously raised in this country, and the return that was furnished the other day indicated-there is no dispute about it-that the former Speaker of this house, now Senator Lemieux, did continue to exercise control over the expenditures of this house until the meeting of parliament in September last. Under those circumstances that answer is part of the records of parliament that he so controlled those expenditures. It is said that the statute enabled him to do so. It may be that that is the proper interpretation of it. I am not expressing any opinion at the moment. I had my attention directed to it by several correspondents who wanted to know who was Speaker of the House of Commons and how control and direction of the staff should be continued by a gentleman who had been removed from our midst and appointed to the upper chamber.
I would point out that the question in the form it is asked is not libellous. It does not insinuate or assert that public moneys have been spent; it asks if certain pieces of furniture were taken to the summer residence of the Speaker.

speechtext: Surely you must read the second question with the first. I am bound to say with the right hon. gentleman that I would prefer that the question had not been there, but I do not think it is a question that can be summarily disposed of in that way. I will give the reason why-the further question, "Who paid for the transportation of the said furniture?" My right hon. friend says that that question and question No. 3 are not sufficiently inquisitorial, that they are statements rather than questions, and with that view I confess I do not wholly disagree except that the questions should be read together as a whole. I quite agree the question as a whole should be now dropped from this order paper. I feel that the third and fifth questions should be preceded by the words "if so." Those questions, in terms, are not different from the questions which appear in courts of equity on interrogatories. I certainly think that the question can properly be dropped, but I desire to say very emphatically that there is no uncertain view held by many people in this country, and I am one of them, as to how the direction of the expenditures of this house and its administration could be carried on by one who had ceased to be a Speaker and had become a senator, and who immediately after actively participated in an election campaign and made a speech, the offensiveness of which will never be forgotten by many people.

A couple of years ago a

That was made by the provincial government, with the two railways cooperating.

Perhaps that is so, but
at any rate it is a provincial government report, because it has never been returned to us. It is in their hands and they are dealing with it. Then there is the survey made by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company on their own behalf. The three reports have to be coordinated, if we may use that word, or brought to some common relationship before any decision can be arrived at. I think it would be talking at a loss to discuss this matter, at least until after the proposed conference is held between Sir Henry Thornton, Mr. Beatty and myself.

In view of the fact that the Canadian National Railway cooperated with the Canadian Pacific Railway and the provincial government in regard to that one survey, it should be tabled, because it involved an expenditure of federal money.

Probably it will be tabled a little later on. I have been in communication with the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson) and with the hon. member for Peace
River (Mr. Kennedy) to whom I stated that I have been in touch with the provincial government but so far they have not given me a copy of the report.
I have no desire to delay my own estimates, but I would like to take up a matter raised last evening by the hon. member for Melville (Mr. Motherwell), in connection with the choosing of Port Nelson as the terminal of the Hudson Bay railway. In replying to an inquiry made by the hon. gentleman I stated that I understood that the responsibility for the choice of Port Nelson was upon both former ministers, Mr. Graham and Mr. Frank Cochrane. The hon. member contradicted me and said that he understood it was upon Mr. Cochrane alone, and without being very sure of my ground and not wishing to put Mr. Graham in wrong, I more or less subsided and agreed with him. However, since last evening I have looked up this matter and I would like to make two or three quotations from Hansard of 1912 and 1913, which will show that the responsibility was upon both these hon. gentlemen. I think it only fair to the memory of Frank Cochrane to show that the responsibility for the choice of Port Nelson was shared by Mr. Graham. I will quote only the relevant passages from Hansard, and my first quotation will be from Hansard of March 21, 1912, page 5763, as follows:
Mr. Graham: If I remember correctly, the information I had, it pointed to this-that Nelson harbour would be by far the best so far as the railway is concerned and the railway operations.
Mr. Cochrane:	Yes.
Mr. Graham: No question about that.
And Mr. Graham continues:
I prophesy that Port Nelson will be the harbour. I know that my hon. friend knows that it is a mistake to prophesy, but prophesying about harbours-well, of course, that is different.
And then Mr. Cochrane continues:
As to the port, as I have already said, I hope to be able to make a decision in a couple of months. Port Nelson as the hon. gentleman (Mr. Graham) says would be much preferable for one reason, at least-it is 85 miles shorter.
In Hansard of 1913 there are some quotations of Mr. Frank Oliver, now an officer of the railway commission, which show that he took the attitude that Churchill was the better port. I will not read these quotations, but for the information of hon. members they appear on page 10940 of Hansard of 1913. The following appears on page 10947 of Hansard of 1913:

Has the minister any information as to what the rates on grain will be from Fort Churchill to Europe?

That question has been gone into by the officers of the department and by some of the steamship officials of the Canadian National Steamships, who have met in my office. I cannot give any conclusive answer but I can say that some steamship companies have indicated that they would be willing to send ships into Fort Churchill and carry grain from there to Europe at a rate somewhat higher but not extravagantly so than the Montreal rates. But of course the whole question is made more complex by the fact that insurance enters into it to a very marked extent, because of the insurance rates were very high, it might counteract any advantage accruing from the shorter haul from the prairies via Churchill to Europe. I do not think an intelligent answer can be given to my hon. friend until later in the season when we have made arrangements perhaps for some private company to take grain via that route.

I may assure him that we are doing the best we can to have a private company handle the whole proposition. May I say at this point that unless some private company does this, and unless we can give a proper estimate of what the cost will be, this will not be a fair test of the port. Of course a shipment this fall will not be a fair test, but it will be the best we can do this year. Any action by the Canadian government itself in absorbing the necessary charges involved in the trial shipments would not constitute a fair test of the route. I can assure my hon. friend-perhaps that is all he wishes-that we have the matter in hand; we are working on it and we shall endeavour in plenty of time before the test is made in September, to have arrangements entered into whereby a shipment or shipments will be made from Churchill.

Does the minister think this
will be the means of diverting much of the Canadian freight that at present goes through t'he United States?

Of course, the whole question depends upon what the ultimate rates will be. If the rates are lower than the present competing rates, naturally a good deal will be diverted. If the rates should happen to be higher, it is natural that the diversion will not be great. Only time can tell what the rates will be and what the answer to my hon. friend's question will be.

When Fort Churchill
was finally decided upon as a port, I understand that certain expropriation proceedings took place with regard to particular lands. Have those expropriation proceedings been completed and payments made?

It was in 1927 that expropriation proceedings against the so-called Beech property at Churchill were instituted and a test case to determine the compensation to be offered went before the Exchequer court at Winnipeg in 1928. The decision of the Exchequer court, rendered on March 24, 1929, established a value of $30 a lot. The result of that has been that to date 45 owners have accepted that amount of compensation and have given the crown title to 156 lots out of a total of 1,406 lots. We have received many protests from people who bought the lots at a much higher price when they were put upon the market by Mr. Beech and his associates, but the judgment of the Exchequer court is final and fixes the compensation at $39 a lot. When I was at Churchill last year I saw the property and I know something of real estate values or perhaps I should say,
lack of values, because I went through a boom or two myself, and I think the award of 830 a lot was very generous.
I presume the balance of the lots will be turned over to the government in due time?

I have just received a
letter from one of the owners stating that he is not willing to turn his lots over. However, they have been expropriated and the only question remaining is what compensation shall be paid the former owners. When that has been cleared up such property as is not required for Dominion public works will be handed back to the province of Manitoba as part of the crown domain.

The delay will not hold
up development of the port?
They are so far away from the port that no interference at all will be caused.
How far away are they?
About three and a half to four miles from the docks.

Towards the ocean or the
other way?

Well, the ocean is all
around. I would say the other way.

Does the government own
all the townsite of Churchill?

The land has all been
given back to the province of Manitoba with the exception of the Beech property, a strip along the railway running through the town, and the industrial sites on the water front. The strip. 250 feet wide, on each side of the railway, the industrial sites along the water front, a lot for the wireless and a few others, including the Beech property, required for various purposes by the government are still owned by the Dominion government, but outside of these they have all been turned over to the province.
Mr. BEAUB1EN:	Has the Beech estate
received payment for those lots?

For the lots which they
have been willing to accept settlement for on the basis of the Exchequer court award, but some of the Beech heirs have refused to accept the award, which carries interest at 5 per cent from the date of expropriation. Of course there can be no settlement with the former owners until they accept the award and give title.

As a member for a northern riding of Saskatchewan I am pleased to hear the minister is doing his best to complete the road as an operating unit, to build up the harbour facilities and to provide storage facilities at Fort Churchill for western grain and other goods. It seems to me that a very important matter and one which has been brought to the attention of the minister is the insurance rate across the north Atlantic and the price which it will cost to take the grain from Fort- Churchill to the markets of the old world. It is not necessary to say that western Canada, especially Saskatchewan and Manitoba, is at the present time, taking just as big an interest in this problem as it has done for the past ten or fifteen years and will until this route has been absolutely tested and the result given to the farmers and citizens generally of western Canada.
Last night I heard an hon. member speaking about the number of days which the port has been open during a certain number of years.
I believe that those tests of the past ought to give place to the tests that will take place in the future. It is what we shall find to be the facts during the next four or five years, after shipping has commenced from that port, that will mean something. These figures are all right, but what the west wants now is a real test of that route. The west wants not only the facts concerning the route and con-

lerning that port in particular but we want, to know everything possible regarding shipping conditions across the north Atlantic to the ports of the old world. We want the essence of these facts in connection with western development fully made known. While I am on my feet I would like to ask the minister if he has given any consideration to the question of holding a suitable official celebration when Churchill port is opened?
No.

Some of the hon. members on the other side of the house seem to 'become excited whenever the port of Churchill is mentioned. I think they had better get their sentiment boiled down because they will have plenty of opportunity to get excited from now on as the development of the port proceeds.
What did your government do?

What did it not do? I am asking if the minister has given any serious consideration to the matter of holding a suitable celebration when the port of Churchill is opened?
By that I do not necessarily mean a western celebration but one of a national character. When the port is opened the attention of all the people of Canada should be concentrated upon it, because in connection with that port, so far as the west is concerned, history of far reaching importance is going to be made. I do not know whether or not the minister has considered the question I have brought to his attention. We westerners look at the port from a national point of view. We do not look at it just from the standpoint of Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Regina, Saskatoon, Prince Albert, North Battleford or any other area. We take a national view, and it is from that aspect that we wish to have it tested. We want the minister and the government of the day to do their utmost to bring about a one hundred per cent development of this port because westerners are looking forward to the day when the new port will play an important part in building up the purchasing power of western Canada and help to develop to a greater degree than ever that portion of the Dominion.

I have tentatively decided that to carry on to a successful conclusion the work at Churchill this fall in time to make even a test shipment of grain, will necessitate the very best efforts of our engineering department and contracting companies. For that reason any celebration or

Supply-Railways-Hudson Bay
official opening of the port would be more fittingly held in 1932. In other words if we endeavoured to do too much this summer we would perhaps be accused of delaying the test shipments we hope to get out this fall. Great effort will have to be put forth to get the test shipments out because the contract for the erection of the elevator does not call for completion until September 15 and there are not many days between that date and the close of navigation in those regions. Therefore there would not be very much time left to come and go on. For that reason I think it would be wise to leave anything in the nature of an official celebration or opening until the following year. I think that would meet with the approval of all hon. members.
I would like to clear up another point. Various companies have applied for industrial sites and for rights to ship certain goods through the port of Churchill. Some of the applications have been made for advertising purposes. The companies in question wish to be the first to ship goods through that port. Other applications are made on commercial grounds. However, owing to the amount of work which will have to be done between now and September 15 we are making a general rule that these companies will have to wait until 1932. If we allowed private corporations to use the port and interfere with it probably we would not be in a position to get out the test shipments this fall. We do not wish to be accused of delaying the test shipments; if possible we would like to get them out.

Probably the Mafeking cut-off will be built in another year and a shorter route will be available?
Mr. MeINTOSH: I am thankful to the minister for his explanation in connection with the question I asked concerning the official opening of the port. I think he Is well advised to hold the opening over for another year; next year would be a very suitable time. My point is however that when the official opening is held it should be made an outstanding event.

May I ask the minister if it is the intention of the government to allow any private grain companies to establish elevators at that port, or if it is the intention to keep the port open for public elevators only?

Up to the present time we have had no applications from any private companies to establish elevators at the port. Until applications are made we will not have to make a decision on that point. If the matter came up I do not know to what conclusion I would come. Frankly, I have not given any thought at all to the question; it will have to be decided when it comes before me.
Before the matter concerning elevators is decided there should be some discussion in the house.
Why not have it now?

I thought it would be better to have the discussion when we were considering the estimates of the Department of Trade and Commerce for the grain commission under whose control I suppose the elevators would be?

No. The elevator we are building at the port is under the control of the Department of Railways and Canals. Ordinary supervision carried on by the Board of Grain Commissioners for all elevators in Canada naturally will be effective in connection with the elevator at Churchill. The management of the elevator however and the general operation of it will be under the control of my department.
Is not the licence issued from the Department of Trade and Commerce? Have they not control over it through the grain commission?

I do not know about the licence. The Board of Grain Commissioners have a supervisory right over all the elevators in Canada. They supervise the operations of all elevators from the standpoint of seeing that everything is carried on according to law. However the erection and operation of an elevator may be carried on either by a private company, by the government, by the Department of Trade and Commerce or by the Department of Railways and Canals. My hon. friend knows as well as I do that there are many private elevators as well as those under the Department of Trade and Commerce and the Department of Railways and Canals.
The licence would have to be granted through the grain commission?
I do not know about that.

There should be ample
opportunity given in this house to discuss the necessity of keeping Churchill free from private elevators. In connection with the operation of the new Canada Grain Act as consolidated at the last regular session of parliament, those of us who spent a great deal of time on the matter would like to see Churchill left with nothing but public elevators so that we could check up the other ports which have both private and public elevators.

There is a private company at Winnipeg which is very anxious to build a stockyard. It is not so anxious about elevators as is my hon. friend. We are prepared this year to make a trial shipment out of Churchill and I hope the minister is making some arrangement whereby a stockyard will be provided to help out the situation regarding freight rates to European markets. Another hon. member sitting on this side of the house and myself were living in western Canada when this road was started by Hugh Sutherland many years ago and we are very anxious to see the completion of port facilities for the betterment of the movement of grain as well as live stock out of western Canada.

It is not possible this year to provide facilities for the shipment of live stock. I repeat what I said a minute ago in answer to my hon. friend on the other side of the house that we are going to find it difficult enough this year to get out the last movement of grain and there will be no opportunity to ship live stock. The success of the port of Churchill however does not depend on trial shipment this year of grain or live stock. Its success depends on shipments in the next year and in years to come. In 1932 there will be ample opportunity for my hon. friend and his associates to build stock yards there, and we shall be very glad to have him come along with a proposition. We will certainly give it our very best consideration.

May I say for the benefit of the minister that if he will permit a trial shipment this year to show that the route is feasible, the farmers will go more into live stock so they will be ready for 1932. I am getting along in years, and I do not want to wait any longer. I have waited 45 years to see the completion of this road.

It is impossible for us to provide shipping facilities for live stock this year. I regret this, but it is simply out of the question to attempt it. My hon. friend says he is getting along in years, but nobody thinks he is; everybody thinks he is a young man. I have not the slightest doubt that he will be with us in 1932 and help us to ship live stock out of Churchill.
He is looking younger than ever.

Is any restriction put on

Not a new contract; a
continuation of the old contract. We spent the money after we came into power.

No, I do not think so. I see the amount for 1931-32 is $3,000,000. Does the minister contemplate that there will be any occasion to spend more than that money in the present fiscal year?

May I answer first the
reference of my right hon. friend, but not in any controversial spirit. I am informed by the department that, for example, on the

Supply-Canals-Welland
Hudson Bay railway contract nearly $2,000,000 was overspent on one occasion and the late government paid it. I am not criticizing this, I am simply pointing out it has been the custom to let the work go beyond the amount voted in the estimates for the year, and it is provided for in the supplementary estimates next year. In this work most of the contracts are on a unit basis. I have a list of the contracts here; most of them go back several years. According to the advice of the legal branch of my department, the contractors could go on and complete the contracts when they will, because they are supposed to complete the work in a certain time anyhow, but generally speaking the amount of money provided in the estimates is the amount that our engineers reckon will be needed that year. But last year was exceptionally fine from the standpoint of the contractors, and they were able to get an amount of work done which would have exhausted the estimates for that year a good deal earlier than usual, and in September or October they would have laid off a good many of their men. Consequently it became a question whether they would continue or not, and they decided to continue and the extra money was provided in the supplementary estimates. This year the vote of $3,000,000 will not be sufficient to cover the completion of the canal; about another $4,000,000 will be needed for this purpose. I may say quite frankly that I am not positive from a legal standpoint as to the position of some of the contractors in that regard. Some of the contracts call for the completion of the work this year, so it is obvious that if the contractors chose to go on with their work, irrespective of our ruling in the matter they might do so, but they would have to wait until the money was voted to pay them. If they insist in going on after the appropriation is exhausted they must wait until further money is appropriated next year.
They do it at their own risk.
Yes. Some of the contractors might insist on going on, and probably we would not object so long as they were prepared to wait for payment.

That comes
down to the question of control of the House of Commons over matters of expenditure. I think the minister ought to give the contractors to understand that this is the amount *of money parliament will appropriate for this year unless he increases that amount by a sum in the supplementary estimates.

They understand that
already.

It would be
unfortunate if in regard to these expenditures, running into millions, it becomes the general practice of contractors to think they can go ahead and incur obligations beyond the specific amount that parliament has voted with any certainty of the moneys being paid later on. I hope the minister will keep that point in mind.

The contractors have already been notified as my hon. friend suggests. They know the amount that is in the estimates this year; they have been told so, and their position is not a bit different from what it was in previous years, because they have always been in exactly the same position, as far as I am advised. Their contract, for example, is for so many million of yards of dredging, which would take a number of years to do, and no contractor knowing he could get only $1,000,000 this year would go ahead to the extent of $10,000,000 unless he saw a prospect of getting the money within a reasonable time. This year the condition is different in this way, that the work is nearly finished. One contractor took the matter up with me the other day. He said, "1 have $500,000 worth of plant on the job at the present time, I have $100,000 of work to do to complete my contract. Am I permitted to go ahead and do this if I wait until next year's estimates for my money?" I did not want to give him a definite answer. But I think it will be generally agreed that it would be hardly fair to him or to any other contractor to tie up his $500,000 worth of plant this year or next year until he completes the work. I do not think there is anything irregular in what is being done so long as the contract price is not altered in any way; and all these prices so far as I know were established by my right hon. friend's government; we have not changed them or the contractors. I repeat, I do not see any irregularity about the contractors going on with the work if they wait for their money.

Carried to its logical conclusion, my hon. friend's argument would do away with the necessity of estimates altogether. The estimates amongst other things are for the purpose of giving members of parliament an idea of how much money is to be spent on the different enterprises each fiscal year and definitely to limit that expenditure within that period of time. It raises the larger question which we were discussing

last night, as to the attitude which members from other parts of Canada may take with respect to these great capital expenditures in localities other than those from which they come. Here is an expenditure of 83,000,000 this year, and S9,000,000 last year, on the Welland canal, and there is an expenditure of 86,000,000 for the Hudson Bay railway. I should think hon. member's from British Columbia,, for instance, might reasonably expect that their constituents would ask, "What has become of the Peace River outlet? That is the matter of transportation which affects us. How do you justify your voting so many millions for the Hudson Bay Railway and so many millions for the Welland canal, with nothing for a much-needed addition to the transportation system of British Columbia, particularly when it has been specifically mentioned in a pledge given by the Prime Minister with respect to transportation generally?"
My hon. friend said a moment ago I might speak on the Welland canal, or at least any canal, and perhaps this would be an opportune moment to say a word with regard to the St. Lawrence waterways as another part of the large transportation scheme which has been outlined and pledged by the Prime Minister as part of the policy of the present administration. That scheme in its entirety was set out in what has been called pledge No. 5 of the Conservative party, as enunciated by the Prime Minister at Winnipeg. It reads as follows:
We pledge ourselves to the improvement of the whole scheme of Canadian transportation-
Then it divides the scheme as follows:
-northward by the completion of the Hudson Bay route, and the construction of such branches as may be necessary to render it most readily available to every part of Canada; to the Pacific slope by a Peace River outlet, and east and west by the development of the St. Lawrence waterways, and we pledge ourselves to aid existing traffic channels and to increase port facilities on the great lakes, Hudson bay and the Atlantic and Pacific oceans, and to the establishment of a national highway system.
It seems to me all those various projects should be taken together in considering the estimates, and I submit that it would be proper to discuss them together, as being relevant to each other, if there is a desire so to do. Quite clearly the scheme that is set out is a vast transportation scheme relating in part to the Pacific, in part to the Atlantic and in part to the northern region as well as to the great St. Lawrence system, and in order to have these projects properly promoted, it does seem to me that as between the different parts of Canada there must be some relativity in the matter of expenditure, so that one por-

tion will not necessarily receive more consideration than the other.
May I ask my hon. friend whether he can give us, at this stage, a statement with respect to the St. Lawrence waterways, as to what has been done by the administration up to the present time to implement the promise given that the government would immediately proceed with the St. Lawrence waterway development? I think I could give my hon. friend the exact words of the pledge in that regard. Speaking at Cobourg on June 24, as reported in the London Free Press of June 25, the Prime Minister said:
If elected we will take up the St. Lawrence waterway and complete it at once. There have been nothing but promises from Mr. King.
I should like to ask if there has been anything but promises, up to the present, from the Prime Minister.
I think there has been 3 good deal besides promises from the present Prime Minister; I think he has done a great work so flar since he came into power.
I am speaking now of the St. Lawrence waterway.

As far as the St. Lawrence waterway is concerned, as my hon. friend well knows, this is an international and a national-provincial matter. It is also a matter for the state of New York. All these different parties are interested, the provinces, the state, the Dominion, and tihe federal government of the United States. I cannot tell my right hon. friend, as he well knows-because he was Minister of External Affairs for a long time-anything about communications passing between the government at Washington and my right hon. leader, but such communications have passed, according to my information. I cannot say as to the exact position of the matter, -but I understand that arrangements still remain to be made between the two governments, and perhaps between the state of New York and this government or the state of New York and the federal government of the United States. There are these different understandings to be brought about before anything can be done.
So far as the actual construction of the canal is concerned, I would say it has not progressed very much since we came into power, and las far as that promise goes, my right hon. friend knows very well that once arrangements are made it will take some eight to ten years at least to complete the canal. This is too important a question, I should think, on which to arrive at a decision in the course of a few months. A vast amount of

Supply-Canals-W elland
money is involved, and I am sure my right hon. friend will agree that sufficient time should be taken to see that proper arrangements are agreed upon before any final decision is made. I do not say this in any spirit of recrimination, but my right hon. friend had the matter under consideration, and he dealt with the United States for a long time. I remember asking him several times in regard to the status of that question, and in the nine years my right hon. friend was in power not a great deal of headway was made. All that my
hon. friend has said with regard to the St. Lawrence waterway involving international problems and the like is exactly in accord with what I said, and is the reason I gave as explaining why, up to the time at which I was speaking, greater progress had not been made. The present Prime Minister, however, took issue with that method of proceeding-I thought at the time most unwisely-and stated he would proceed at once. I thought he would have been well advised, in view of the great responsibilities which lay before him in connection with the many promises which were made, if he had said quite frankly that this was a vast undertaking, with a great variety of considerations of the kind which my hon. friend has just mentioned, which would take a little time to work out, but he did not do that. The Prime Minister said that the government of the day had not been proceeding with the matter because they did not wish to do so. The Prime Minister spoke at several places with regard to the St. Lawrence waterway. For example, at Winnipeg on June 9, he said:
Has anything been done to the St. Lawrence waterway? Why?
He continued:
Because it was the business of the government to do it and the government did not choose; they did not dare.
That was not the reason. The reason that more progress was not made was exactly the reason mentioned by my hon. friend, and I think in his reply he may possibly have been quoting from what I said. The Prime Minister, however, said it was because the government did not wish to go on with it, and elsewhere he made similar statements. Speaking at Cobourg, on June 24, as reported in the

London Free Press of June 25, the Prime Minister said:
If elected, we will take up the St. Lawrence waterway and complete it at once. There have been nothing but promises from Mr. King.
Then at St. John, as reported in the St. John Telegraph-Journal of July 1, he said:
We offer you the St. Lawrence waterways; the Chignecto canal is a possibility, yea, even a probability.
The right hon. Prime Minister made all these pledges with regard to the waterway. He said the work was to be proceeded with at once. If I understand the minister aright to-day, he is telling us on behalf of the administration that he is unable to make any announcement about what has been done up to the present time. He says there may have been some corespondence between the government and Washington, but I imagine there has been no more than one exchange of communications. Beyond that I do not think the minister could indicate anything else, and it is nearly a year sance this promise was made.

My right hon. leader is Minister of External Affairs, and whatever communications are had with Washington naturally would pass through his hands. He has not made any public Statement, and any other statement of his naturally would not be for publication. So I am quite sure my right hon. friend has an opportunity any day, on the orders of the day, to ask my right hon. leader as to further communications with Washington, as he has done already on one or two occasions. Of course there is this to remember, that the criticisms my right hon. leader aimed at the right hon. leader of the opposition during the election had to do with lack of action over a period of nine years. It is hardly the same thing to criticize him for lack of action over a period of nine months. There is a difference of some twelve hundred per cent in the two periods of time. I hope everything will be satisfactorily arranged and the canal built, not at once, but within a reasonable time.

My hon. friend forgets that during the period of nine years all the ground work was carried out and everything done in preparation for immediate action. There had to be international commissions and advisory bodies both in the United States and Canada to go over the preliminaries of the whole project. All of that work was successfully cleared up in the period in which the previous administration

It could be built and operated without danger to our sovereign powers, and with every safeguard to provincial rights. Throughout the different branches of my department we are gradually putting all employees on the eight hour day basis. There are some employees who work more than eight hours a day-watchmen, for example. But we are gradually putting them on the eight hour schedule.

I think my hon. friend

Now, it would cost the government something extra to change the contracts with a view to having the employees who are now operating under the old contracts put on the eight hour day schedule. I would point out that inasmuch as Canada was a signatory to the peace treaty, and inasmuch as we have adopted an eight
hour day, the government might consider the reconstruction of these contracts with the object of paying the contractors the additional amount required to enable them to put their employees on the eight hour day basis.

Should the contracts be changed, naturally the government would have to pay the contractors a sum to cover the extra outlay, but inasmuch as Canada has now adopted the principle of the eight hour day, I think the government could very well consider having this principle put into effect in respect to the rest of this work. Had I been over on those benches, which I fortunately am not, I would have recommended to my colleagues that this great national undertaking, the Welland canal, might very well be completed on the eight hour day principle. It would not cost very much, and I think for the honour of Canada the principle should be adopted in relation to what still remains to be done.

If there is no item upon which certain discussion may be had which hon. members desire to enter upon, they will have the opportunity to propose an amendment when the motion is made to go into committee of supply. If there is no such motion and no particular item in the estimates to which the subject can be related, the discussion must not take place.

Surely when an examination of the estimates before the committee discloses the fact that certain work is required for which no item appears, the question ought to be allowed as to why no provision for it has been made in the estimates.

I have just a few remarks to make with regard to two orders which have been issued by the railway board. The first order is No. 45205. On May 1, 1929.
The general manager of the Atlantic region of the Canadian National railways wrote the secretaiy of the chamber of commerce of Riviere du Loup stating that the Canadian National railways were willing to build a station at that point. There is also a letter from the principal assistant to the president of the Canadian National railways,- Mr. Hummel, dated May 28, 1930, which appears in Hansard of March 31, at page 528. There is also a letter from Mr. Fraser to the joint secretary of the railway board, dated July 12, 1930. I have only a translation here, but in the letter it is stated that in the Canadian National Railways budget there is an item for the construction of a new station at Riviere du Loup. There was also a letter from Mr. Rand, general counsel for the Atlantic region of the Canadian National railway,
stating that they were anxious to have the work proceed without undue delay. That letter, dated July 14, 1930, also appears in Hansard of March 31, at page 481.
Tenders were received at Moncton on August 26. The order of the board appears at page 614 of Hansard for April 15. I note that this order is dated August 9 of last year, after my hon. friends came into power, and that order was in accordance with the general policy of the Canadian National Railway. On September 19 the minister told the house the matter was under consideration, and nothing was done until October 7, when the Canadian National Railways notified the tenderers that their cheques would be returned to them owing to the fact that the Department of Railways and Canals had refused to sanction the construction of the station. That letter also appears in Hansard for March 31, at page 531.
I wired the Minister of Railways on October
14,	a few days after the refusal to construct the station had been announced. That telegram appears in Hansard for March 30 at page 421. On the following day I received an answer, which appears on the same page of Hansard. Then on November 3 of last year a resolution was passed by the city council of Riviere du Loup, which appears in Hansard of April
15,	at page 615, and which was acknowledged by the minister as follows:
(Translation) I beg to acknowledge receipt of your letter of the 4th inst., also of a certified copy of the attached resolution.
The construction of the new station at Riviere du Loup will bo a question submitted at the inquiry, at the same time as other requests of a similar nature. Your town was not specially signalled out when the subject came up.
I especially draw' the attention of the house to this remark.
It was intended to construct a number of public buildings at various places in the district, however the work was not proceeded with owing to the decrease in business.

I have the honour to be,

That resolution was also sent to the Board of Railway Commissioners, who answered on November 6 that the matter would be investigated.
On December 9 the assistant chief engineer of the operating department of the Canadian National railways wrote an interesting letter to Mr. Alistair Fraser, assistant general counsel for the Canadian National Railways. I might refer for a moment to the wire from

my hon. friend the Minister of Railways under date of October 15, in which he says that necessary repairs to the station have been sanctioned. At the time the minister came to that decision there was an order of the Board of Railway Commissioners approving the plans for a new station. This was a new policy inaugurated by the Minister of Railways, in contrast with the general policy of the Canadian National railway in that connection.
In answering the resolution of November 3, which has appeared in Hansard, Mr. Hazen, of the Canadian National railways reported as follows to Mr. Alistair Fraser:
With reference to your letter to Mr. Appleton of the 14th ult., enclosing copy of resolution passed by the city council of Riviere du Loup and forwarded to the board of railway commissioners, regarding our station at that point, and your memorandum to me of the 5th inst., file 723-6, asking to be advised as to what answer should be file with the board.
It is quite correct that the railway called for tenders for a new station at Riviere du Loup, but these were entirely too high, and it has therefore been decided to thoroughly renovate the present structure in order to meet the requirements of the travelling public.
Dealing more particularly with the various points raised in the above mentioned resolution, I would advise as follows: Paragraphs 5, 6, 7 and 8 (size of station and hygienic conditions).
The present structure, with certain interior revisions, is considered to be large enough for present traffic conditions, and the hygienic conditions complained of will be rectified by completely renewing, with modern equipment, the toilets and lavatories including the installation of tiled walls and flqprs, hot water, and improved lighting facilities.
In the public waiting-room terrazzo floors will be installed, lower parts of walls tiled, and upper parts plastered, together with improved lighting facilities.
Upstairs, it is the intention to remove the sheathing from the walls, and replace same with lath and plaster; new hardwood floors will be installed, and all toilet and lavatory fixtures to be renewed along modern lines. The exterior of the building will have the brick-work cleaned and pointed, and woodwork painted.
The building, as a whole, is structurally sound, and it is considered that its complete renovation, both interior and exterior, with slight revisions, in the layout, will make it in all respects a station entirely in keeping with the requirements of the community, and in first-class condition from a hygienic standpoint.
Paragraphs 12, 13 and 14 (unemployment relief program).
No item was included in our agreement with the government for the relief of unemployment, to cover any work at Riviere du Loup station.
It is the intention to carry out the improvements outlined above at the earliest possible date, and it is felt that when same have been completed there will be no cause for further complaint.
Sgd. H. T. Hazen,
Assistant Chief Engineer, Operation Dept.

This time, apparently, the Canadian National Railways have changed their policy in accordance with the policy of the Minister of Railways in respect to this matter. I waited some time and on January 15 I wired as follows to the secretary of the railway board:

The Secretary,
Railway Commission,
Ottawa, Ont.
Your letter, December 24. F36455 Riviere du Loup station, letter Hazen to Fraser, December 9 does not include construction of cellar. Repairs not sufficient. New building required from every viewpoint.
What was amazing in the report of the railways was the statement that "when the proposed repairs were completed there would be no further cause for complaint." But that memorandum made no mention of any cellar nor of improved foundations and so forth. The railway board answered my telegram on January 16, saying that they would look into the matter. On December 27 I had written to the minister asking for some information about the work to be done and on January 19 I wrote him as follows:

T beg to thank you for your favour of the 14th instant.

On January 26, 1931, the railway board forwarded me a letter from Mr. Alistair Fraser, general counsel of the Canadian National Railways. That letter, dated January 23, 1931 reads:

Replying to your letter of the 16th instant; there is already a cellar under Riviere du Loup station measuring 39 feet 6 inches in length by 23 feet 6 inches in width, located under the

second-class waiting room. The floor area is slightly over one-third of the area of the whole building and is ample to take care of all purposes.
This basement is used for furnace, coal bin. and battery room, and when recently inspected was dry and in good condition.
Yours truly,
Alistair Fraser.
But in the spring and fall there is considerable water in that cellar, which is only about one-third of the floor area of the building, as the railway officials admit.
I wrote to the railway board, telling them about the condition of the cellar, of the foundation and of the sewerage system, and they answered me again to the effect that they were taking the matter into consideration.
On January 30, Dr. Lessard, director of the Board of Health of Quebec, wrote to the secretary of the railway board, and the letter will be found at page 482 of Hansard. The report attached to that letter has not been given to this house and I will take the liberty of reading it:
(Translation)
Emile Nadeau, M.D.,
Associate Director,
Provincial Health Bureau,
Parliament Building,
Quebec.
Sir,-
I have the honour of submitting to you the report of the inspection on the cellar and sewer system of the Riviere du Loup station, as requested by your letter dated the 21st inst.
Cellar: It comprises a space of 40 feet in length by 23J feet in width and 6i feet in height, on an average. The walls and floor are made of cement. The ratio of the area of the cellar with that of the building which is properly _speaking the station (128 feet in length by 27£ in width) is 1 to 4; the remaining part of the station is on an average 2 feet above the ground. In the cellar are located the furnaces, the coal-bunker, a room for wet batteries, a very large chimney, three brick pillars, a staircase and the various pipes in connection with the sewer and heating systems.
Four shafts 21 feet by 2 feet each, on an average, provide light to the cellar; there is a door for the coal; there does not seem to be any means of ventilating the place, according to the station staff, in the spring, during the rainy season, water filters through to the cellar.
Sewer system: the main pipe lies at one end of the cellar, on a level with the floor. A drain in the cement floor carries the water to the said main pipe, of which the intake end is not closed, this unfortunately allows noxious gases to escape through the cellar.
Two other drain pipes-A.B.-are connected with this main pipe, as shown on the sketch.
The pipe A drains the urinal, a toilet room and a sink; we are told that very often this drain pipe is blocked up, owing to the fittings being badly done.
The pipe B which drains a number of water closets has nothing noticeable except it is hard
to repair, owing to there being only a space of 2 feet, on an average, between the ground and the floor of the station almost throughout its length.
We noticed that when we inspected the place there was a leak in the water pipe.
In brief, I doubt that one can say there is a cellar, when its space covers but one-fourth of that occupied by the building, the sewer system moreover is really defective.
(Signed) J. C. Beaudet, M.D.,
Medical Officer
Riviere du Loup, Jan. 28, 1931.

Following our previous correspondence, I have sent you last week the third instalment of the story of the intrigues made by some people to prevent the building of a new station at Riviere du Loup.

Dear Doctor Manion,-
Pray find herewith enclosed copy of my letter of February 16th and of the enclosures,
As you have wired me on October 15th ult. that the necessary repairs to Riviere du Loup station had been sanctioned and as the proposed repairs by the Canadian National Railways do not include the construction of a cellar therein nor any improvement in the present sewer system nor repairs to the foundation, be kind enough to let me know at your earliest convenience if it is your intention to reconsider the decision of your department regarding the immediate construction of a new station at Riviere du Loup.

to have fair play. I do not understand how the Board of Railway Commissioners could have for the same reason rescinded not long ago a decision that they had given on the 9th of August. What has been done is most unfair, and in the name of all my constituents, independently of party, I ask him kindly to see to it that the Canadian National Railways adhere to their first proposal, which would give fair treatment to the people of Riviere du Loup.

On section 1-Line of railway authorized.
Mr. JOSEPH A. MERCIER (Laurier-Outremont):	Before this clause is passed 1
should like for a few moments to make certain observations in connection with it. Through this bill the Canadian Pacific Railway asks permission to construct a certain line of railway. Clause 1 of the bill is as follows:
The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, hereinafter called "the company," may within two years after the passing of this act commence to construct a line of railway from a point on the company's railway between Breslay station and its terminus at Place Viger in the city of Montreal, county of Hochelaga, thence in a generally northerly direction through the counties of Hochelaga and L'Assomption, to a connection with the company's railway at or near L'Epiphanie, all in the province of Quebec.
The distance between Place Viger and Breslay Stations is about five miles, figuring in a direct line. By the railway it takes twenty minutes to go from Place Viger to the Mile End station, which is in my division, and I would say that the Breslay station- which by the way is the new station under construction by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company at the northern extremity of Laurier-Outremont-is possibly one mile farther away than the Mile End station, making the distance between the Place Viger station and the Mile End station six or seven miles. The railway company may construct this line at any point over this distance of six or seven miles. The northeast section of Montreal has a sufficiency of railway lines, and we who represent the people in that section of the city, which is very densely populated, are opposed on general principles to the construction of any further lines. Speaking more particularly of my own division, I wish to emphasize the fact that there are no vacant lots in the northeast section of Laurier-Outremont. The Canadian Pacific Railway is doing a good work in the construction of the new Breslay station on Park avenue and Jean Taillon streets; much benefit will result in the furtherance of the development of this northern part of the city. I understand the station is to cost about a million and a half dollars, and that it is a handsome structure which when finished will reflect credit upon the part of the city in which it is located.

Canadian Pacific Railway BUI
The question of building this line came up before the railway committee on Wednesday and Thursday of this week. Certain amendments were offered to the bill but were not accepted by the committee. The company submitted a plan on which was indicated the probable line the railway would take. The plan of construction has not yet been prepared, and before the committee the company had no definite plan to offer. As I have stated, the company merely indicated on a map the general direction in which the line was to be constructed. On the plan presented appeared a line in heavy red ink about three-quarters of an inch wide was all that indicated the location of the new line. Mr. Flintoft, the attorney for the company, was asked if that red line indicated any particular point on the present railway line between the Place Yiger station and the new Breslay station from which the new line would start. He answered that as yet no plans had been prepared but that the map before the committee simply showed the general direction in which the line was to run, and that the company did not know at which particular point the new line would start. I suppose if the Canadian Pacific Railway is spending over a million dollars for the construction of a new station in the north end of Montreal it intends to use it to the greatest extent possible. The Breslay station is in a direct line immediately south of the station at L'Epiphanie in the county of L'Assomption where the projected line is to join the main Quebec line of the Canadian Pacific Railway. If the company takes the shortest distance between Breslay station and L'Epiphanie the line will pass right through the heart of Laurier ward in my constituency, one of the most thickly populated sections of the city of Montreal, with the result that the property owners in that section of the city will have their property ruined because this is to be an elevated railway. The company, through its attorneys, stated before the railway committee on Wednesday that it was not its intention to build an underground or depressed line owing to the cost of such construction, but that it was its intention to build an elevated road. This means that the property adjoining the projected line will be of no value and we shall be faced with a situation similar to that which confronted us in connection with the construction of the new terminal facilities of the Canadian National Railways, which involved elevated lines into the city of Montreal. As representing one of the divisions of that section of the city, I am strongly opposed to the passing of this bill until such 22110- 121J
time as the plans are submitted to the committee in order that we may know the exact location of the line. As I said at the outset, the Canadian Pacific Railway has other lines in that section of the city, and it could very easily make use of its existing lines in the construction of this short cut to Quebec. We are all in favour of shortening the line to Quebec, which is one of the heavily travelled lines of the Canadian Pacific into the Montreal district. I understand that by going directly through l'Epiphanie there will be a saving of some fourteen miles. It is only natural that the company should desire to shorten its line, but there is no reason why the same serious situation as arose in connection with the Canadian National Railways should be created in this case, and I submit, Mr. Chairman, that the committee should not pass this section until such time as plans are submitted showing the exact location.
I am availing myself of this opportunity to express my dissent in the hope that the electors in that part of the city which I represent will be made aware of the intention of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and will in turn voice their dissent to the construction of the proposed line. I repeat, I hope the committee will not pass the section.
Mr. ST-PERE (Translation): Mr. Speaker, the few remarks which I intend to make with reference to clause 1 of Bill No. 15, will be, so to speak, but a repetition or a second edition of those that I made before the railway committee, Wednesday last.
Clause 1 reads as follows:
1. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company, hereinafter called "the company," may within two years after the passing of this act commence to construct a line of railway from a point on the company's railway between Breslay station and its terminus at Place Viger in the city of Montreal, county of Hochelaga, thence in a generally northerly direction through the counties of Hochelaga and L'Assomption, to a connection with the company's railway at or near L'Epiphanie, all in the province of Quebec; and may within five years after the passing of this act complete the said line of railway, and if within the said periods respectively, the said line of railway is not commenced or is not completed and put in operation the powers of construction eon-iferred upon the company by parliament shall cease and be null and void as respects so much of the said line of railway as shall not then have been commenced or completed, as the case may be.
The fact that said line will follow a certain route in the county of Hochelaga obliges me to oppose the adoption of this clause. I wish to state, sir, that the county of Hoche-

Canadian Pacific Railway Bill
laga and especially that part of my riding which includes Hochelaga and Prefontaine wards, is at present diagonally crossed from the southwest to the northeast by the Canadian National line which runs between Moreau street station and the city of Quebec. This line in use for a number of years runs through church and school areas. Let me point out that it is a serious impediment to traffic, a constant danger to pedestrians and school children, that religious and school authorities, property owners and residents of these two wards of my constituency in Montreal, strongly oppose the building of this line -either as a level, overhead or underground line. It may be somewhat of a surprise to hon. members to hear the member for Hochelaga protesting against the construction of this new railway because many think that a new line almost invariably contributes to the prosperity of the district it crosses. I must say that we think differently and following instructions forwarded to the member for Hochelaga on behalf of property owners, tenants, and the authorities previously mentioned, nothing in the world will induce me to vote in favour of such a clause.
There is another railway which crosses the centre of Prefontaine ward. This overhead line was built by the Canadian Pacific railway and has never been in use owing to the protests made at the time by the city council of Maisonneuve. This line which passes through the centre of this section, like those located south of Ontario street, has been for a number of years detrimental to the erection of new buildings. It was greatly responsible for the depreciation of property in that part of my constituency, and the pillars of this overhead line are a constant danger to automobiles.
Mr. Speaker, owing to the protests which I received, because of the vague wording of this clause, which does not specify the starting point of this line, I must, on behalf of the residents of that section of my constituency, acquaint the house that in order to comply with the objections raised by my constituents, I shall be obliged to vote against clause 1 which requests the construction of a new line which will be, so to speak, but a branch of the present one.
At the last meeting of the railway committee, I was somewhat astonished when a letter received from Mr. Fairweather, of the Canadian National Railways, was read, offering, as a solution for this new difficulty, to allow the Canadian Pacific the use of the present Canadian National lines. May I remind Mr. Fairweather that, in 1929, when the Palmer scheme was discussed in the railway 
committee, Mr. Brown, chief engineer of the Canadian National, gave his word so as to meet my wishes and that of one of the councillors of that section of my constituency, that the freight passing over the Canadian National line in Hochelaga and Maisonneuve would only be put in the sheds at night when the building of the central terminal of Lagauchetiere street would be completed. Can we suppose that this pledge will be carried out if the Canadian Pacific Railway accepts the offer just made by Mr. Fairweather? Then, what would become of the pledges given to the member for Hochelaga and the councillor of the Prefontaine ward when the Palmer scheme was discussed in 1929? The people are at present opposed to the freight being put in the sheds during the day, because this delays the traffic of motor vehicles at the numerous railway level crossing gates which are almost invariably closed. Can one reasonably suppose that my constituents will accept such an arrangement? I therefore oppose, on their behalf, the building by the Canadian Pacific Railway of any new short branch between Montreal and "Epiphanie," if this line is to cross the wards previously mentioned. As stated before I strongly object, because such a line would depreciate property, prevent landlords renting their houses advantageously, because it would be a constant source of danger for pedestrians and school children, would delay traffic, and finally because far from contributing to the general prosperity of these two wards, it would be a burden for that eastern section of Montreal included in my constituency. For these reasons I shall vote against clause 1 of Bill No. 15, intituled An Act respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway.

Mr. Speaker, not being a member of the railway committee, I had not the opportunity of studying and discussing this clause which gives to the Canadian Pacific Railway company the right of constructing a railway from a point located on the main line, between the Breslay station and the terminal at Place Viger station. I wish to strongly protest against clause 1 because the construction of this line would only serve the interests of that railway company and in no way those of citizens residing in the various sections that said line is to cross. This railway will be built through the centre of Montreal and will cross the best sections, Laurier-Outremont, my constituency (St. Denis) and also Hochelaga and Maisonneuve, counties which are at present well provided for. I therefore do

Canadian Pacific Railway Bill
not see any good reason for authorizing the Canadian Pacific to build this line of railway.
Neither can I understand why the company, in its request did not specify the exact starting point; it only mentions "a point located between the Breslay station and the Viger station." Why not specify the exact starting point of this line and thus avoid creating uneasiness among those who object to having their section crossed by a railway which would depreciate the value of their property. As representative of the county of St. Denis, wholly settled and inhabited by a population which has made great sacrifices to comfortably house themselves, I must protest in order to safeguard the interests of the citizens of my constituency preferably to those of the Canadian Pacific company. I would not like to see a railway cross diagon-alljr my county, from the northeasterly boundary to the southwesterly one passing through the beautiful parish of St-Edouard, then across the lovely parishes of St.-Am-broise and St-Jean-Berchmans. I ask hon. members of this house, to fully consider this clause and to reject it. The clause under discussion is not couched in precise language and we should not, by our vote, give a blank signature to this company which will use it to destroy the sections which form a beautiful background to the city of Montreal. In the northern and southern parts of Montreal we have sufficient railways to provide for the population. If the Canadian Pacific Railway needs to shorten its line between Montreal and Quebec, it seems to me that it could come to an agreement with the Canadian National Railway Company, so that trains might utilize the new line which the latter w-ill build in the northern section of the city, instead of disfiguring the picturesque and artistic appearance of Montreal, as well as depreciating real estate in that part of the city. For all these reasons, sir, I strongly protest against this clause and I must ask hon. members of this house to withhold their approval from a move tending to depreciate sections which are an element of beauty, greatness and prosperity for the city.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to associate myself with my fellow-members, as the representative of the lovely county of Maisonneuve which is situated at the extreme eastern end of the Montreal island.
The proposed railway would no doubt cross the county of Maisonneuve, although its location is very indefinite. The Canadian Pacific Railway Company intends, according
to this bill, to construct a line from a point-located between the Yiger station and that-of Breslay, thence mostly in a northerly direction. The north is not specified, whether it be the magnetic or true north; however, if the starting point be near the Viger station, the whole centre of Montreal will be crossed in a northerly direction, if on the other hand, the starting point is near the Breslay station, it will be impossible for the line to take a northerly direction in order to reach the county of 1'Assomption, it would necessarily cross the county of Terrebonne. I therefore contend that the committee cannot accept clause 1 in respect to the building of a line through the city of Montreal.
The section of my constituency which would be crossed by this proposed line is partly urban and partly rural.
There is already the proposed railway line of the Canadian National which is to cross that part of my county, however this railway will not extend as far as that of the Canadian Pacific because the Canadian National line would be built towards Longuie-Bointe so as to join the main line there, while the Canadian Pacific Railway seems to want to build much further north and would thereby cross prosperous farms and thus be very detrimental to farmers. The committee should not accept such an indefinite clause. Let the railway company submit its plans to us and we may judge then whether our people can approve this scheme. I would be pleased to second the efforts of the Canadian Pacific Company at this time of depression,-if the construction work began soon it would certainly relieve unemployment,- however, for the reasons given it is impossible for us to accept clause 1 as at present worded.
