Before you take the vote, Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word. I thought some other hon. members were going to speak, or I should have been on my feet before you called for the yeas and nays. I have in my hand a letter from the Canadian National railways which was read before the committee, at which I had not the opportunity of being present because I was out of the city. The attitude of the Canadian National railways is expressed in this letter, written by the counsel of the Canadian National railways to the counsel of my department:

Canadian Pacific Railway Bill
For the information of the minister and of the railway committee. I have to advise you that the Canadian National does not propose to appear to offer opposition to Bill 15, entitled, "An Act respecting the Canadian Pacific Railway Company."
We desire to suggest, however, that the territory, through which will run the very indefinitely described line specified in section 1, is or will be served adequately by lines of the *Canadian National now existing or under construction and that what appears to be economic waste on proposed new construction can be avoided by securing through running rights (the same as they gave us at Port Arthur) if the same be necessary, over the national lines.
In other words the Canadian National itself is not opposing this line, therefore from the standpoint of the two railways there is no reason why anyone-I am speaking now to justify my own vote, because I intend to vote for the bill-should vote against it. But may I say that I sympathize with my hon. friends who have spoken representing that section of the city of Montreal which will be affected. They do not wish their whole city cut up by various railway lines. I also sympathize with the idea expressed in this letter that we should not permit unnecessary duplication of railway lines. We all know that that sort of thing in the past has to a large extent brought about the sad condition of railway affairs in Canada today, and it should be the duty of all members of this house and of all citizens of Canada to avoid as far as possible any further duplication.
Therefore I undertake on behalf of the government to suggest, in writing, to the Board of Railway Commissioners that before the plans of the Canadian Pacific Railway are approved by the board-which must be done in connection with all plans of that kind -the board give an opportunity to the city of Montreal and other interested sections of *Quebec to appear before them and show [DOT]cause why the Canadian Pacific Railway, if it builds this line, and the Canadian National Railway, in connection with lines it has built or is about to build, should get together and obtain common running rights for the two roads over the one line. That appears to me the sensible position to take.

That is a good
explanation; the bill was explained that way in committee.

This bill did come before the committee, as the hon. member says, though I was unable to be present. The committee accepted it, but in view of the fact that the government are quite willing to .take that attitude towards the two railway

companies and ask the board to give an opportunity to all concerned to show why unnecessary duplication should not take place, and why the two roads should combine and receive common running rights, I think this bill might pass.

Are they not bound to give that opportunity in any case?
Mr. MANION; No, I do not believe so. However, to avoid any misunderstanding I will put myself on record as suggesting to the board, on behalf of the government, that this opportunity be afforded.
There was a suggestion in the committee that the bill should be amended to make the city of Montreal and other interested districts parties to the case, but that suggestion was not accepted.

If the government requests the Board of Railway Commissioners to give Montreal and other interested districts an opportunity to appear in this matter, the Board of Railway Commissioners would hardly dare take any other course. I suggest that under these circumstances, the committee, in view of the fact that the Canadian National Railways are not opposed to the bill, and in view of what I have stated on behalf of the government, accept the bill. I do not think there will be any difficulty whatever if these two railways get together and share running rights on terms suitable to both and approved by the Board of Railway Commissioners.

I was a member of the railway committee where this bill was discussed, and I think I ought to say a word or two. I was not able to follow the hon. gentleman who spoke in Frenoh, but I did follow the hon. member who spoke first. He reechoed the objections which were raised in the committee, the most serious of which was the fact that the city of Montreal was not a party to this application. It was pointed out to them, however, that under the Railway Act, as administered by the Board of Railway Commissioners, it was obligatory to hear all who made representations regarding any application for a charter. It has been suggested that the line is indefinite. Well, I have followed with interest, both before and after I became a member of this house, the granting of charters here, and a't no time have I ever known of a railway that was surveyed and a definite route plan kid down before the charter passed through this house. This line is in exactly the same position. As

to whether it should be an elevated railway or underground, or a surface railway, that is a matter of policy within the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners, who will suggest to the Canadian Pacific Railway just where the line should go. This bill was thoroughly discussed in the railway committee, and in order to be consistent I shall certainly have to support it.

As sponsor of the bill I might say a word with reference to the objection of the city of Montreal. Mr. Flintoft, the solicitor for the Canadian Pacific Railway, has already written the city of Montreal, agreeing to furnish them with plans, maps and all other material necessary to enable them to be heard before the board. The city of Montreal is therefore safeguarded. As has been said, this bill was before the railway committee. There were two hearings and the city of Montreal was represented by its solicitor and, as well, by the mayor. I might read the section of the Railway Act which is of importance in connection with this discussion:
Provided that any complaint made to them-
That is, the Board of Railway Commissioners.
[DOT]-shall, on the application of any party to the complaint, be heard and determined in open court.
Objection has been made that in some Canadian National case this was not done; but, as I have stated, the Canadian Pacific Railway, in this instance, has agreed in advance that this course will be followed. I am not personally concerned with the bill; I am merely sponsoring it. As a matter of fact, I live thousands of miles away from Montreal. I do think, however, that the bill ought to go to the proper tribunal, the Board of Railway Commissioners, for consideration.

Mr. Chairman, the minister was to give me some information.

My hon. friend spent some time before six o'clock dealing with a proposal to build a station at Riviere du Loup. May I suggest to him once again that the committee is fully informed on that question, and the matter will be given consideration. The hon. member seems to have the impression that Riviere du Loup is the only place in Canada which has been denied a new station. As a matter of fact, over $8,000,000 worth of additions and betterments of one kind and another for the Canadian National Railways -which sum was voted last year in the estimates-have had to be postponed. In other words, the railway station at Riviere du Loup, which was to cost between $75,000 and $80,000-we will take it at $80,000, to have a round figure-is exactly one per cent of the works which were deferred last year by the railway company; it is just one in a hundred. The hon. gentleman therefore has no right to feel that Riviere du Loup was treated so much worse than many other parts of the country, since projected expenditures aggregating between $8,000,000 and $9,000,000 were similarly delayed. rMr. Neill.]
The other evening my horn, friend asked what had become of the money which, as he said, had 'been voted; why was it not spent on the Riviere du Loup station? Recently he wrote a letter to the Ottawa Citizen in regard to the same question. Let me tell him what became of the money. It was used for some other purpose by the national railways. The national railways have had, in the past at any rate, power to switch moneys voted for one purpose to another. This is a power which has not, as a matter of fact, been possessed by the Canadian government itself, and I do not mind saying quite frankly I do not believe the Canadian National Railways should have this power to any great extent, and certainly not to the extent they have had it in the past. I believe that when appropriations are passed in the house the money so voted should as far as possible be spent upon the item for which it was voted, or it should not be spent at all. Unfortunately, however, that has not been the case heretofore, and I repeat that in the past year between $8,000,000 and $9,000,000 that were voted for certain pur-posese were used for other purposes than those for which the money was voted. I come back again to tell my hon. friend that the case of Riviere du Loup was merely one of those estimates, totalling between SS,000.000 and $9,000,000 which were voted by the House of Commons last year and which were switched to other purposes. I have endeavoured to answer the hon. gentleman's question as propounded in the house a few days ago in regard to what became of the money and I have tried to show him that Riviere du Loup was treated no worse than many other sections of the country.

Riviere du Loup has a very good representative here, and I wish I could fight for my riding as my hon. friend does for Riviere du Loup. While unfortunately Riviere du Loup is not in my riding, I want to point out to the minister that an amount of $1,500,000 was paid out of the unemployment relief fund for the purpose of encouraging the railroads to proced with a program of work which the railroads felt they should not have proceeded with ordinarily for, as the minister said, probably one, two and in some cases as long a time as four years. This was done for the purpose of talcing care of unemployment. Does it not seem bad business to go on with and spend $1,500,000 on work that will not be required for three or four years when they could have spent $50,000, $60,000 or $75,000, I do not know how much, in one portion of the country

Supply-Riviere du Loup Station
where a station has been burned down, and thus enable the commerce of that section to be handled properly?

Let me correct my hon. friend. The station at Riviere du Loup was not burned down. In any case the works in regard to which the government gave this one and a half million dollars to meet interest charges, were works proposed by the Canadian National and Candian Pacific Railways themselves. A meeting was held in my office, later in the office of the Minister of Labour, and railway officials were present. An understanding was reached that they would submit a program of works on which the government would pay the interest for a year or a year and a half in view of the fact that the railways were doing the work in advance of the time that they would ordinarily have done it. The railway officials went away, worked over their plans and later submitted them; but I regret to say that among the works which they proposed to do, they did not include the station at Riviere du Loup to which my hon. friend refers. It was never discussed: it was never proposed, and so far as I know, it was never thought of. The matter was not brought to my attention at all. We agreed to the works which the railways themselves proposed, and which they said were the most suitable ones to carry out under the conditions imposed.

I quite appreciate the fact that neither the Minister of Railways nor the Minister of Labour could think about the station at Riviere du Loup when the railways presented their program of work; but, on the other hand, it might have occurred to someone that the amount required for this station had already been voted under a previous administration, and it is strange that not knowing anything about the territory the railway companies could plan a program of work to. relieve unemployment in other parts of the country when they could not spend in my hon. friend's riding money already voted for work to be done in it. I take it for granted that there Was unemployment in that riding.

The same thing applies to Prince Rupert. Last year an estimate was passed for $250,000 for an hotel. Since then the national railways found it necessary to spend money in Vancouver, so we are still hoping for $250,000 to replace the corresponding amount that they have spent in other parts of the country.

I appreciate very much what the ex-Minister of Labour has said.
He is a former railway employee, and if next summer he visits Riviere du Loup, I am sure he will receive an ovation from the people connected with the railways and, indeed, from all the people of that district. I also thank the Minister of Railways for his kind words to-night. I am glad to see that he is in a good humour at this sitting.
Will he get an ovation too if he visits Riviere du Loup?
That depends on what he will do in the future. If my hon. friend visits us, we shall find a nest for him.
Another one than that which the hon. member has for himself.

A bird should not speak;
it should sing. The Minister of Railways said that the railway officials did not discuss the question of a station at Riviere du Loup when the matter of unemployment relief came before him. The question of the station at Riviere du Loup was before the minister. At the time it was decided, the hon. gentleman was not present, and the acting minister was the hon. member for Argenteuil. But according to the report of the Dominion director of unemployment relief at page 4:
On September 30, 1930, by order in council P.C. 2292, the Minister of Labour was authorized to enter into an agreement with the Canadian Pacific Railway Company and the Canadian National Railways, whereby there would be expended by these railway companies the sum of approximately $25,000,000 in the performance of certain works, and the purchase of certain material over and above the normal expenditure of the said railways, such works to be commenced immediately and to be completed within the ensuing fifteen months.
The date of the order in council-please note it, Mr. Chairman, because it will interest you-is September 30, 1930. Then, an agreement dated October, 1930, was signed by the Minister of Labour and the Canadian National Railways. Clause 1 of that agreement reads as follow's:
Now therefore, it is agreed by and between the parties hereto as follows: First to assist in relieving unemployment the company will undertake and carry on to be completed on or about December 31,	1931, the works more
particularly described in the schedule hereto attached, or such other work-
And I would ask hon. members to take note of the w-ords "other work."
-or works in lieu thereof as the parties hereto may agree upon at the estimated cost of $5,654,748 as set forth in detail in the said schedule.
There was also an agreement signed by the Minister of Labour and Mr. Humphrey, for the vice-president of the Canadian Pacific

Supply-Riviere du Loup Station
Railway, on October 14, 1930. The order in council was passed on September 30, and the agreement between the Minister of Labour and the Canadian National Railways amounting to several million dollars was dated October 1. The agreement between the Minister of Labour and the Canadian Pacific Railway was dated October 14. I would ask the committee to note that the refusal of the minister to sanction the construction of a new station at Riviere du Loup took place on October 7.
I have before me an interesting letter sent on November 6 by my hon. friend the Minister of Railways to the city of Riviere du Loup. A resolution was passed by the city council on November 3 and is recorded in Hansard, to the effect that a suggestion should be made to the Minister of Railways that some moneys be taken from the unemployment fund to complete the difference between the amount voted by parliament and the lowest tender, an amount approximating six or seven thousand dollars. That resolution was passed by the city council of Riviere du Loup and was certified to by the secretary treasurer and the mayor. I should explain that the mayor is the perpetual Tory candidate in my constituency. Naturally the Minister of Railways was very much surprised to see the name of that gentleman on a resolution asking for money. Naturally the minister was surprised that a resolution should be signed by the mayor of Riviere du Loup asking for money for a new station from the unemployment fund. The minister should have known that that gentleman was in Ottawa on October 7 when the Minister of Railways refused to sanction the building of the station. I think my remarks will explain the illuminating letter from the Minister of Railways and Canals to the city council of Riviere du Loup, which says:
Yotre cite ne fut pas proposee d'une maniere speciale lorsque la question fut presentee.
The English translation is, "Your city was not represented in a special way when the question came before us". I congratulate the hon. gentleman on this letter. He wrote when under the influence of indignation, and undoubtedly he was very much surprised to see that the man who blocked the building of the station was interested in one of the tenderers who could not secure the contract. As the gentleman I have in mind could not secure an advantage for his protege he blocked the whole thing so that the community at large would suffer. He was not the right man to go before the minister and ask him to act in accordance with that resolution. As

the mayor of Riviere du Loup he was bound to sign the resolution. He could not go before the people and show his game by saying, "I will not sign it, because on October 7 I blocked it". The minister said plainly not only to the secretary-treasurer of the city of Riviere du Loup but through him to the whole community, that if the city had been represented in a special way the matter could have been arranged. It was not necessary to propose it to the minister. The only course was to let the matter follow its natural course. That would have been done if no obstacle had been put in a previously smooth path.
Did the hon. member say "icicle"?
I am not paying any attention to the hon. gentleman.
The hon. member got the cold shoulder, so he must have said "icicle".

My hon. friend makes a noise but that is all. When I was young I used to hear the noise of fire crackers, and that noise meant as much as the noise now made by my hon. friend.
I shall now read the last paragraph of a letter appearing in Le Saint Laurent on December 31, 1931.
In closing your remarks, you say you are interested in the welfare of our city and you contend that I had sufficient influence to undo in two months what you allege it took you six years to accomplish. You thereby admit that you cannot get the present government to accede to your wishes. Do you wish to prove that you have really at heart .the interest of our city? Resign as member. In a month I shall have replaced you, and I promise that the station will be built within two years, not a sketch of it, but the building itself. I promise to do more in two years than you have done in six. According to your contentions which are often wrong, I have enough influence to prevent the construction of the station. Then were I a member, would I not have enough influence to build the station?
Yours truly,

The first order was dated

The tenders were received on August 26, about two weeks after the date of the first order of the board. Earlier in the evening while a bill regarding some railway project in Miontreal was being discussed, the hon. minister stated that he would write a letter to the Board of Railway Commissioners to ask them to give an opportunity for certain interested parties to appear before them. The hon. minister, perhaps inadvertently, let fall an expression which I do not think he would like to remain on Hansard in its pristine sense. He stated that if he wrote that letter he was sure the Board of Railway Commissioners would not dare to do anything else than to accede to the request contained therein, and give an opportunity to these parties to attend the sitting of the board. I am afraid there is a tendency to think that the board is some sort of adjunct to the government or some department of the government. Let me remind my hon. friend-he knows it as well as I do, and I am sure he will take these remarks in the spirit in which they are given-that the Board of Railway Commissioners is a court of record and, as I remember the Railway Act, it acts only on the direction of the government when an order in council has been passed and a special question has been referred to it. Otherwise, the board acts on its own initiative or upon the application of the parties interested in the matters before it. I do not think it is well to have it get abroad in this country that a government or a member of a government can write a letter and thereby' have the Board of Railway Commissioners take a certain course in connection with their judicial functions. I say that only because it seemed to me that the assurance which the hon. gentleman gave to the hon. gentlemen interested in this bill appeared to be more of an assurance than it really was, because my hon. friend has no more power-I say this with all due respect -to write to the Board of Railway Commissioners and influence their decision with regard to who shall appear before them, than any other hon. member. The very foundation of the jurisdiction of the Board of Railway Commissioners lies in the fact that they are a court of record and a judicial body', and they take cognizance of matters before them just as the supreme court does.

all concerned.

I wish to say a few words in regard to appropriations for national railway purposes. I do not wish to delay the minister's estimates; for I should like if possible to see him complete them to-night. The minister, however, did speak rather freely in regard to the use the Canadian National Railways might make of moneys appropriated with respect to maintenance and operation. The matter is of too much importance to pass without comment, and that is my sole reason for speaking at the moment. To make clear what I have in mind, the minister will agree with me that as regards appropriations such as we are making at the moment no minister would be at liberty to take any sum appropriated for a specific purpose here mentioned and use it for some other purpose. My hon. friend agrees with me in that; it is a fundamental principle of the control of parliament over public expenditure. I submit that the Canadian National Railways is simply one branch of government; it is a nationally owned institution, and its estimates should be presented to the committee of parliament that has to consider them in precisely the same form and be governed by exactly the same principles as estimates of the departments of the government itself. It is entirely wrong for the railway management to take appropriations for particular purposes and divert any part of them to other purposes. I can understand it may be a matter of convenience to the railway management to be able to do that, but it would be entirely wrong if such a principle were adopted in regard to public funds appropriated in connection with any department of government, and I do not see why the Canadian National Railways should be made an exception in that regard. I go a step further: the fact that parliament has not quite the same control over the Canadian National Railways as it has over matters that come more immediately before it in itself constitutes a reason why in making appropriations for the Canadian National Railways for specific purposes we should be even more exacting in requiring that they be applied only to those specific purposes.
There ought to be a distinct understanding on the matter, and I suggest that the minister discuss it with the management of the Canadian National Railways and mention that the subject has been brought up and discussed in parliament. It is certainly a matter with respect to which, speaking for the opposition, I can say we fqel very strongly. The House of Commons has no more important function than that of exercising the closest scrutiny

over public expenditures, and this function can be exercised only where appropriations are made for specific purposes and applied exclusively to those purposes. I have in my hand Durell, the standard authority on parliamentary grants. One paragraph will sum up what I have in mind. I think it should be as applicable to the Canadian National Railway estimates as to our own. Durell says:
When making the grant, parliament appropriates it to the particular vote, and it cannot legally be applied to any other vote though, in the case of the army and navy,-
This has reference to Great Britain.
-transfers between votes are in certain circumstances permitted, parliamentary sanction being subsequently obtained. Generally speaking, however, the money voted by parliament is granted for a particular vote only, and it is therefore clear that the larger the number of the votes, the greater control parliament is able to secure.
The fact that in the main parliament is exercising its control over the Canadian National Railways through a committee of the house is, I sulbmit, all the more reason why the railway management should submit its estimates in as much detail as possible, the appropriation should be made as specific as possible, and nothing in the way of switching or diversion to other purposes should be permitted.

I rise to make a suggestion, Mr. Chairman. As a minister who has sat on appeals from decisions of the Board of Railway Commissioners it has been borne in on me that the governor in council is not the proper body to hear such appeals. This is no reflection on the legal attainments of the gentlemen who happen for the time being to 'be members of the government, because they do give serious consideration to the appeals that come before the governor in council, but I must say they have not the time to give proper consideration to such appeals. In looking up the records I find that usually council has ordered a reference back to the board. This causes delay that sometimes is very detrimental to the people who are interested in securing a readjustment of rates or some other matter. I suggest that the government consider the advisability of transferring these appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada, or else make the judgments of the Board of Railway Commissioners final. I think my hon. friend will agree with me that members of the government have not time to give the required attention to such appeals.

I agree entirely with what my hon. friend says in that regard. Certainly the governor in council is not a rate-making body and has not the technical knowledge to deal with appeals of this nature. But I have been informed that council has never changed an order of the Board of Railway Commissioners; as my hon. friend stated, it has always referred the case back to the board for rehearing. I suppose the appeal to the governor in council is a relic of the days when there was no board of railway commissioners. The board, I understand, was appointed in 1903, previous to which time such regulatory control of railway rates as existed was vested in the railway committee of privy council. I think my hon. friend's suggestion is worthy of consideration !by the government.

Before such a step is taken I submit the matter should be given very careful consideration. I quite agree that rate-making is such a technical matter that few laymen are competent to deal with it. But there are times when questions of rates in a large way may have a very direct bearing on public policy, on the development of certain parts of the country or of certain lines of business, and that aspect must not be lost
sight of. In other words, there are times when more than the mere complexity of rates must be considered. I for one would be very sorry to see the appeal to the governor in council dispensed with until the matter has been very carefully considered.

The matter just referred to undoubtedly is very important. The hon. member who just spoke has, if I may be permitted to say so, the proper conception of the functions of the governor in council in connection with these so-called appeals. I had occasion to look into the matter a little while ago, and I came to the conclusion that "appeal" is scarcely the proper term. The governor in council is not sitting as a court; it is not exercising judicial functions; it does not have to act on any evidence. When the governor in council hears and decides upon the so-called appeals it is exercising executive or administrative functions, and can take into account broad matters of policy as a government. We are accustomed to speak of these appeals as if they were appeals to an appellate court, such as the Supreme Court of Canada, but if that were the case of course the governor in council could not deal with them as they could be dealt with, for instance, by the Board of Railway Commissioners. There can be no question about that; members of council have neither the time, the training nor the experience to .deal with matters in that way.

Nor the
patience.

My right hon. leader adds
that they have not the patience, either, to deal with them. My hon. friend who spoke last has raised a very important point, as to whether at certain times the governor in council should not, as a matter of governmental policy, come to decisions not upon scientific rate-making principles but as executive acts. This is a matter worthy of very careful consideration before that power is taken away. I think the minister is quite correct in saying this is a relic or hang-over from the time when the railway committee of the cabinet dealt with rates. That, I believe, is historically correct, but at present these rates do not need to be determined upon judicial principles at all.

Of course no change can
be made without amendment to the Railway Act, so there will be plenty of time for consideration. At the same time, I would remind my hon. friend that while the privy council has not taken on the judicial powers, they could do so at any time.

I merely suggested this short method of dealing with appeals, which are vexatious and which, as far as I can discover, never have led anywhere.

I wish to call the attention of the minister to the condition of affairs in western Canada. Hon. members will recall that the crop of the west was fair last year but losing prices were received.
